specPoints.text: know that the weight of a body acts through its centre of gravity

primer.text: You have just met moments — the turning effects that forces produce about a pivot. Whether a force turns an object depends on where that force is applied, which raises a natural question: where on a body does its weight actually act? This note answers that with a single special point, the centre of gravity, and shows how to find it.

lessons.title: Centre of gravity
sourceHeadings: Finding the centre of gravity of symmetrical objects
lessons.opening: Every object has one special point at which its weight can be treated as acting — the centre of gravity. Knowing that point tells you exactly where to start the weight arrow in any force diagram. This lesson defines the point, places it for symmetrical shapes, and works through the hanging method used for irregular ones.
keyPoints: An object's centre of gravity is the single point through which its whole weight acts.
A symmetrical object with uniform density carries its centre of gravity at the point of symmetry — a sphere's sits at the exact centre.
An irregular object's centre of gravity is found by hanging the shape from a pivot.
A plumb line hung beside the pivot marks a vertical line that must pass through the centre of gravity.
Repeating the suspension from two further points, the centre of gravity appears where all the lines intersect.
Because the point is hypothetical it can lie outside the body, yet force diagrams must still show weight acting from it.

low.restatement: The whole weight of a body can be drawn as one arrow acting through a single point, the centre of gravity.
low.analogy: A shopping bag swings from one spot on your hand however unevenly it is packed — the bag behaves as if all its weight pulled from that spot.
low.examPointer: In any force diagram, start the weight arrow at the object's centre of gravity — examiners look for exactly that.

medium.restatement: Symmetry locates the point for regular bodies — a uniform sphere's sits at its geometric centre — while irregular shapes need hanging, plumb lines and intersecting marks.
medium.analogy: Hang a picture frame from one nail and let it swing: it settles only when its heavy point hangs directly beneath the nail, which is the settling a plumb line records.
medium.examPointer: The point is hypothetical — it can fall outside the body and slides as posture changes, yet diagrams still anchor the weight there.

check.stem: The centre of gravity of a body is the point through which its:

options.text: Mass is measured
options.explanation: That describes mass, not weight.

options.text: Volume is centred
options.explanation: Volume says nothing about where weight acts.

options.text: Weight is taken to act
options.explanation: This matches the definition of record.

options.text: Surface area is greatest
options.explanation: Surface area plays no part in the definition.

check.stem: A uniform sphere has its centre of gravity located:

options.text: At its exact centre, the point of symmetry
options.explanation: Symmetry puts a uniform sphere's point at its exact centre.

options.text: On its lower surface, closest to the ground
options.explanation: Gravity pulls through the body, not along its surface.

options.text: Halfway between its centre and its surface
options.explanation: Nothing offsets the point from the middle in a uniform sphere.

options.text: Nowhere — a sphere has no centre of gravity
options.explanation: Every body with weight has a centre of gravity.

check.stem: An irregular shape's centre of gravity can be located by:

options.text: Dividing its mass by its volume
options.explanation: Mass over volume gives density, not a location.

options.text: Balancing it on a fingertip
options.explanation: Fingertip balancing is unreliable and not the method of record.

options.text: Measuring its outside dimensions
options.explanation: Length and width do not locate the weight point.

options.text: Suspending it from a pivot and using a plumb line
options.explanation: Suspension with a plumb line is the prescribed technique for irregular shapes.

check.stem: In the suspension method, the centre of gravity is found where:

options.text: At the first pivot used
options.explanation: The pivot is only a hanging point, not the answer.

options.text: Where all three drawn lines cross
options.explanation: The three traced verticals meet at the centre of gravity.

options.text: At the heaviest-looking corner
options.explanation: Appearance does not locate the point.

options.text: Halfway along the plumb line
options.explanation: The plumb line only marks direction; it is not the answer itself.

check.stem: Which statement about a centre of gravity is correct?

options.text: It must always sit inside the material of the object
options.explanation: It is hypothetical, so it can sit outside the material.

options.text: It stays fixed however the body's posture changes
options.explanation: It shifts whenever the body's shape changes.

options.text: It can fall outside the body and move when the shape changes
options.explanation: Correct — a hypothetical point may lie outside and travel as the shape alters.

options.text: Only symmetrical objects possess one
options.explanation: Every body with weight has one, regular or not.

check.stem: State what is meant by the centre of gravity of an object.
check.modelAnswer: It is the single point through which the object's whole weight acts.

check.stem: Describe how to find the centre of gravity of an irregular shape.
check.modelAnswer: Suspend the shape from a pivot and mark the vertical direction with a plumb line hung beside it. Repeat from two further points; the centre of gravity lies where the drawn lines intersect.

check.stem: Explain why the weight arrow in a force diagram should start from the centre of gravity.
check.modelAnswer: The weight is taken to act through the centre of gravity, so an arrow starting there shows exactly where the body's pull is applied. Starting it anywhere else would place the force at the wrong point.

check.stem: A student suspends an irregular card from one pivot, draws a vertical line, then repeats the process from two more pivots. State how many lines are drawn and where the card's centre of gravity lies.
check.modelAnswer: Three lines are drawn — the first plus two repeats — and the centre of gravity sits at the single point where all of them intersect.

glossary.definition: The one point through which a body's whole weight is taken to act.
A matching of halves about a line or point; for an even-density body it fixes where the weight point sits.
The point from which the shape is hung while it settles.
A weighted thread that hangs vertically, used to mark the true downward direction when locating the weight point.
An assumed location rather than a physical mark; it can sit outside the material of the body.
